html:
Paleo-Siberian hunter-gatherers is the map's label for the old peoples of northeastern Siberia, from the Yenisei River to the Bering Strait, from about 2000 BCE to 1200. It is a name of convenience: these peoples speak languages that belong to none of the big families around them, and not to one family of their own either.

The main groups in later times:

  • The Chukchi, Koryak and Itelmen of Chukotka and Kamchatka, whose languages are related to each other.
  • The Yukaghir of the far northeast tundra.
  • The Nivkh of the lower Amur River and Sakhalin.
  • The Ket of the Yenisei, the last survivors of a once wider language group.

They lived by hunting wild reindeer, elk and birds, by fishing the great salmon and river runs, and on the coasts by hunting walrus, seals and whales. Some later turned to reindeer herding, which became the Chukchi and Koryak way of life. On Chukotka they lived beside the Yupik, and ideas and goods crossed the Bering Strait in both directions.

Some linguists link the Ket language to the Athabaskan languages of North America, an idea called Dene-Yeniseian. It is widely discussed but not proven.

Over the centuries shown on the map, other peoples moved into their lands: Tungusic reindeer hunters from the south, and later the Turkic-speaking Yakuts along the Lena. From the 1600s Russian Cossacks arrived and forced them to pay tribute in furs, part of the Russian conquest of Siberia. The Chukchi fought the Russians off for much of the 1700s.
